whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the MuleSoft Developer II exam?

personas.label: Experienced MuleSoft developers
personas.description: You have built Mule applications and want to validate your ability to deliver and support production integrations.

personas.label: Integration engineers focused on DevOps
personas.description: You manage build and deployment pipelines and want to demonstrate your skills with Maven, MUnit, and runtime deployment.

personas.label: Lead MuleSoft developers
personas.description: You guide implementation choices and need to deepen your knowledge of data transformation, security, performance, and reliability.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the MuleSoft Developer II exam?
examDifficulty.summary: This advanced exam assumes familiarity with Mule development and focuses on complex transformations, batch processing, security policies, automated deployments, and production performance. Hands-on experience helps connect the configuration choices to operational behavior.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 120 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
70% to pass, which is 42 correct answers out of 60.
Advanced DataWeave: Practice modules, pattern matching, recursion, and nested data transformations.
Production design: Review batch processing, API policies, CI/CD, runtime deployment, and performance patterns.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Build and deploy at least one Mule application through an automated pipeline. Practice MUnit, Object Store caching, VM and Anypoint MQ queues, TLS configuration, and policy configuration. Aim for at least 80% on practice questions and review why each design fits the workload.

examFormat.heading: MuleSoft Developer II exam format
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or in person. Questions cover advanced development and production operations.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Some questions describe high-volume processing, an API security requirement, a deployment pipeline, or a production issue and ask which Mule capability fits.
bestWayToPass: Practice advanced DataWeave: Use functions, modules, pattern matching, and collection operators on nested data.
Build a batch job: Review job phases, record processing, aggregators, and handling for failed records.
Apply API policies: Combine authentication, client access, IP restrictions, and rate limits based on the requirement.
Automate delivery: Understand how Maven, MUnit, API Autodiscovery, and deployment targets fit in CI/CD.

certificationCard.description: The advanced MuleSoft developer exam. Expect deep questions on DataWeave modules, batch processing, API security policies, CI/CD pipelines with Maven, and production deployment strategies. The exam is 60 scored questions in 120 minutes, with a 70% pass mark, weighted towards Implement performant and reliable Mule applications (27%) and Implement maintainable and modular Mule applications and Maven builds (25%).

blocks.heading: Advanced DataWeave
blocks.body: DataWeave supports reusable functions and modules as well as mappings between nested structures. Pattern matching can select behavior based on a value or type. Functions can be named, passed as values, or reused across transformations. Choose map when transforming each array item, reduce when accumulating a result, and mapObject when transforming object key-value pairs. Handle missing and null values intentionally with defaults or conditional logic, and keep complex transformations readable.

blocks.heading: Batch Processing
blocks.body: Batch Jobs process large datasets as individual records through configured steps. The job can include input handling, record-processing steps, and an On Complete phase. A Batch Aggregator groups records for a downstream operation; commit size controls how many records are sent together. Failed records can be tracked and handled separately. Use batch processing for large record sets that do not need one synchronous response, and design for recoverability and operational monitoring.

blocks.heading: API Security Policies
blocks.body: API Manager can apply policies to deployed APIs without embedding the policy logic in the Mule application. Client ID enforcement identifies registered consumers. OAuth or JWT validation checks tokens. IP restrictions limit network sources, and rate limiting controls request volume. Select policy combinations based on authentication, authorization, and traffic requirements, and verify how the policies apply in the target runtime.

blocks.heading: Performance and Resilience Patterns
blocks.body: Scatter-Gather runs routes in parallel and combines their results; it is useful when several independent calls must all complete before responding. A cache can avoid repeated expensive calls for data that remains valid for a configured time. Queues and asynchronous processing can separate the caller’s response time from downstream work. Reconnection strategies address transient connection failures. Choose a pattern based on latency, consistency, and recovery needs.

blocks.heading: CI/CD and Runtime Deployment
blocks.body: A CI/CD pipeline can run MUnit tests, package a Mule application, deploy it to a test environment, and promote it after validation. The Anypoint Maven Plugin and CLI support automated build and deployment workflows. API Autodiscovery links an application to its API definition so API Manager policies can be applied. Configure runtime region, workers, and other deployment settings for the target platform. Design stages and approvals to prevent untested changes reaching production.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the MuleSoft Developer II exam
scenarioTips.intro: For each scenario, identify whether the main concern is transformation, volume, security, latency, or deployment. Choose the Mule capability that addresses it and consider its operational trade-offs.

blocks.heading: Write Reusable DataWeave
blocks.body: Practice modules, functions, pattern matching, recursion, and transformations of nested JSON and XML. Choose collection functions by the output needed.

blocks.heading: Choose Batch or Parallel Processing
blocks.body: Use batch jobs for large record sets processed through steps. Use Scatter-Gather when independent routes can run in parallel and their responses must be combined.

blocks.heading: Combine API Policies
blocks.body: Map the requirement to client identification, token validation, IP access, and rate limiting. Apply policy controls through API Manager where appropriate.

blocks.heading: Plan Runtime Deployment
blocks.body: Compare CloudHub and Runtime Fabric options for the workload. Design deployment, worker sizing, high availability, and rollback or recovery procedures.

blocks.heading: Tune and Protect Performance
blocks.body: Use caching for repeatable results, queues for decoupling, and appropriate polling or thread settings for the workload. Measure changes in the runtime rather than guessing.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Related credentials for MuleSoft Developer II
nextCertsAfter.intro: Continue with a MuleSoft architecture, integration, or platform operations credential.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the focus of MuleSoft Developer II?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Developer II focuses on advanced Mule application development and production deployment practices.
whyWrong: This certification covers production Mule application development.
Basic API terms alone do not cover the advanced developer objectives.
User interface design is not Mule application development.

sampleQuestions.question: Which language is used for complex data transformations in Mule applications?
sampleQuestions.explanation: DataWeave is MuleSoft’s language for mapping and transforming data.
whyWrong: Apex is Salesforce’s programming language.
AMPscript is used in Marketing Cloud content.
Visualforce is a Salesforce UI framework, not the Mule transformation language.

sampleQuestions.question: Which approach is a sound way to handle errors across Mule flows?
options: Use error handlers with appropriate continue or propagate behavior
Use Apex try/catch for all Mule errors
Ignore errors and allow the flow to continue silently
Delete the flow when an error occurs
sampleQuestions.explanation: Mule error handling scopes and handlers let developers define how failures are logged, recovered, or propagated.
whyWrong: This is the recommended approach for handling Mule flow errors.
Apex try/catch applies to Apex code, not Mule flow error handling.
Ignoring errors can hide failed processing.

sampleQuestions.question: Which deployment target can host Mule applications in a managed MuleSoft cloud environment?
sampleQuestions.explanation: CloudHub is a MuleSoft-managed deployment environment for Mule applications.
whyWrong: CPQ is for Salesforce product configuration.
Slack is a collaboration service.
CloudHub is a managed runtime target for Mule applications.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a reusable asset mean in API-led connectivity?
options: An API intended for only one consumer
An asset used once and then discarded
APIs designed for reuse across consumers
sampleQuestions.explanation: A reusable API or asset can support more than one consumer, reducing repeated integration work.
whyWrong: A single-consumer asset does not provide the intended reuse.
An asset used once and discarded is not reusable.
Reusable assets are software artifacts, not physical hardware.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Mule error strategy handles an error and allows the flow to continue?
options: On Error Propagate to fail the flow
sampleQuestions.explanation: On Error Continue handles the error and lets processing continue after the handler completes.
whyWrong: On Error Continue handles the error and allows the flow to keep running.
Without a handler, the error is not explicitly managed.
On Error Propagate returns the error to the calling flow or runtime rather than continuing.

sampleQuestions.question: Why use batch processing in Mule?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Batch Jobs process large datasets as individual records through configured steps.
whyWrong: Email delivery is unrelated to processing a data set.
API creation is separate from processing records.
Batch processing handles large data sets through configured record steps.

sampleQuestions.question: Which DataWeave functions can transform or select array content?
options: Write one value to a variable
sampleQuestions.explanation: map, filter, pluck, and reduce support common collection transformations and selection tasks.
whyWrong: A key lookup is not the set of collection transformations asked about.
These functions support common array mapping, filtering, and aggregation.
Joining strings is a narrower task than transforming array collections.

sampleQuestions.question: What does API versioning help support?
options: Safe migration of clients between versions
sampleQuestions.explanation: Versioning lets API providers introduce changes while maintaining a transition path for existing consumers.
whyWrong: Versioning does not prevent all changes.
Versions let clients migrate while maintaining a compatible path.
Breaking all clients immediately is not a safe version strategy.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Mule component starts a flow on a configured schedule?
options: An HTTP Listener responding to requests
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scheduler starts a flow at configured times or intervals.
whyWrong: An error handler responds to failures rather than starting scheduled work.
A Scheduler starts flows at configured times or intervals.
An HTTP Listener responds to inbound requests rather than running on a timer.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a custom policy in API Manager used for?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A custom policy applies organization-specific checks or controls to API requests.
whyWrong: A custom API policy enforces organization-specific request controls.
Automatic deletion is not the purpose of a policy.
Policies govern API behavior rather than create the API implementation.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Mule scope can manage a transaction when the connector and resource support it?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A transactional scope can coordinate operations when the participating connector and resource support transactions.
whyWrong: A flow is not inherently transactional for every operation.
A Try scope handles errors but does not make every operation transactional.
A transactional scope coordinates operations when resources support it.

sampleQuestions.question: What does idempotency help prevent in an integration?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Idempotent processing lets a retry of the same request avoid creating duplicate business effects.
whyWrong: Retries may still occur; idempotency prevents duplicate effects.
Idempotency helps avoid duplicate business effects when a request is repeated.
It does not remove processing delay or all possible failures.

sampleQuestions.question: Which strategy can reduce downtime during a Mule application release?
options: Stop the old deployment before preparing the new one
sampleQuestions.explanation: A supported rolling or blue-green release can shift traffic while maintaining availability during deployment.
whyWrong: Manual replacement without health checks can create downtime.
A full stop before deployment creates an outage window.
A supported rolling or blue-green strategy can keep service available during deployment.

sampleQuestions.question: What is MUnit used for?
sampleQuestions.explanation: MUnit provides tests for Mule applications and flows.
whyWrong: MUnit is for testing, not only monitoring.
Deployment is a separate lifecycle step.
MUnit tests Mule flows and applications.
